senses.gloss:
āvasathya
(‘related to the dwelling place’)
------------------------------------------
For performing वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्, duly consecrated fires are needed. The maximum number of such fires is five and they are called ‘pañcāgnis.’ They are: गार्हपत्य, आहवनीय, anvāhāryapacana or dakṣiṇa, सभ्य and आवसथ्य.
The word ‘āvasathya’ is derived from ‘āvasatha’ or a dwelling place. According to one view, the ब्राह्मणस् and others who were invited to participate in a sacrifice used to be put up in special dwelling places called āvasatha (similar to a modern dharmaśālā) where a fire was to be lit, to ward off cold. This could have been the origin of this fire.
During वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्, this fire is stationed to the east of the सभ्य fire, in a hut called ‘āvasatha.’ The hearth is triangular in shape, each side being 25 aṅgulis (aṅguli = finger’s breadth).
Some authorities of वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् held its establishment compulsory and others as optional. For establishing it, the original fire had to be brought from the गार्हपत्य.

avāntara-dīkṣā
(‘secondary initiation’)
------------------------------------------
A yajamāna (one who performs a sacrifice) is expected to take दीक्षा or initiation at the beginning of the sacrifice he is undertaking. This is a purificatory ritual which imposes on him certain rules and code of conduct.
Sometimes, as a part of a major sacrifice, minor rites also will have to be performed. Some of these, considered as very important, require the yajamāna and his wife to take an additional दीक्षा. Such a दीक्षा, taken at the beginning of a subsidiary rite which itself is part of a bigger sacrifice, is called ‘avāntaradīkṣā.’ For instance in the अग्निष्टोम (a सोम-याग), avāntaradīkṣā has to be taken before the प्रवर्ग्य rite. The yajamāna and his wife offer fuel sticks into the आहवनीय and गार्हपत्य fires respectively. Touching the water heated in the vessel called ‘madantī,’ the yajamāna clenches his fists closely, tightens his girdle and drinks hot milk. The दीक्षा ends with nihnava, a kind of salutation to हेअवेन् and earth, by the priests.
See also DĪKṢĀ.

āvaraṇa-śakti
(‘veiling power’)
------------------------------------------
According to the Advaita Vedānta as propounded by शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820) the ultimate Reality is one only, the one without a second—ekam eva advitīyam brahma. But that we perceive this world of multiplicity, is a fact of experience. शङ्कर attributes this to māyā or अविद्या or अज्ञान (illusion or nescience or इग्नोरन्चे). This māyā/ अविद्या covers this Truth or ब्रह्मन् and makes it appear as something else which it really is not, viz., the world. For instance, the semidarkness of twilight covers up the real nature of a rope and the semilight projects it as a snake. The power of māyā/avidyā to veil the truth is called ‘āvaraṇaśakti’ and its power to project it as something else, is called ‘vikṣepaśakti.’
Just as bright light destroys the illusory perception of the snake in the rope, even so ज्ञान, knowledge or direct experience of the Truth (Brahman/Ātman) will destroy this māyā/avidyā.

avakīrṇin
(‘one who has violated [the vow]’)
------------------------------------------
A Vedic student living in the होउसे of the गुरु to learn the वेदस् and allied sciences was called a ‘brahmacārin.’ He had to follow a given routine, observe a prescribed code of conduct and keep certain vows. Any violation of these vows, whether intentional or unintentional, had to be atoned by appropriate prāyaścittas or expiatory rites. Violation of the vow of ब्रह्मचर्य or celibacy was the worst of these. The ब्रह्मचारिन् who wilfully had sexual intercourse with a woman was called an ‘avakīrṇin.’ The Dharmasūtras of आपस्तम्ब (1.9.26.8) and वसिष्ठ (23.1-3) as also the Manusmṛti (11.118-121) prescribe that the अवकीर्णिन् should sacrifice an ass to the deity निरृति, which is symbolic of the stupid lapse, wear the skin of an ass for one year, should beg his ड़ोओद् from seven houses announcing to them his lapse, take ड़ोओद् only once in a day and bathe thrice a day. Then only he will become pure. वसिष्ठ substitutes an oblation of boiled rice for the sacrifice of an ass.
See also BRAHMACĀRIN.

āvaraṇa-devatā
(‘deity [installed in the area] surrounding [the main deity]’)
------------------------------------------
The गर्भगृह (sanctum sanctorum) of a Hindu temple is generally surrounded by āvaraṇas or enclosures whose number may vary from one to seven. Though the main purpose of these āvaraṇas is to provide space for pradakṣiṇā (circumambu-lation) round the main deity, they also serve to accommodate the images of other deities considered to be the attendants or the retinue of the main deity. These deities are called ‘āvaraṇa-देवतास्’ or ‘parivāra-देवतास्.’
The Vaikhānasāgama lists as many as 135 परिवारदेवतास् spread over seven āvaraṇas for a विष्णु temple. ब्रह्मा, अनिरुद्ध, त्रिविक्रम, वरुण, शुक्र, बृहस्पति, Subhadrā—these are some of the deities listed there.
In a शिव temple, देवी, चण्डेश्वर and ब्रह्मा find a place in the āvaraṇas.
In a देवी temple, शिव, विष्णु and गणपति will invariably be there. So also कार्त्तिकेय or सुब्रह्मण्य.

avaccheda-vāda
(‘theory of limitation’)
------------------------------------------
According to the Advaita Vedānta ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute is one, without a second. The jīvas or the individual souls, though apparently limited and many, are ब्रह्मन् itself, in the ultimate analysis. How the One becomes or appears as the many is metaphysically indefinable. But it is, however, describable figuratively or analogically. The two well-known theories that have successfully attempted this are: बिम्ब-प्रतिबिम्ब-वाद, also called pratibimba-वाद (‘theory of reflection’) and avacchedavāda (‘theory of limitation’).
According to the former theory, māyā and अविद्या act like reflecting media. When ब्रह्मन् is reflected in māyā, it becomes ईश्वर; when reflected in अविद्या, it becomes the jīvas. Though the reflected images (called ‘pratibimba’) are affected by the media, the original (called ‘bimba’) is not. Also, when one reflected image is affected by the changes in the particular medium, other reflections may not be so affected. This explains the different condi-tions of the different jīvas though all the jīvas are reflections of the same ब्रह्मन्. When the reflecting media are done away with, the reflections too disappear, leaving only the original intact. This view was propounded mainly by पद्मपाद (A. D. 820) and his successors and is one of the characteristic features of the Vivaraṇa School.
In the latter theory, propounded by the भामती School, when ब्रह्मन् the Absolute, appears to be limited by māyā, it becomes ईश्वर; when limited by अविद्या, it becomes the jīvas. A classic example for this limitation theory is the sky or space (ākāśa) and containers like a pot. Though space is unlimited, it appears to be limited by a pot or a room or a होउसे. On the destruction of these limiting adjuncts, space ‘regains’ its original status.
See also ADVAITA VEDĀNTA DARŚANA.

Avadhūtagītā
(‘song of the अवधूत’)
------------------------------------------
The Avadhūtagītā is one of the 36 minor philosophical poems composed in imitation of the well-known Bhagavadgītā. It is an independent treatise on Advaita Vedānta and preaches an uncompromising non-dualism. Its authorship is attributed to अवधूत दत्तात्रेय. Hence it is also called Dattagītā or Datta-गीता-yogaśāstra. It is also titled, though rarely, Vedāntasāra.
This small treatise of 271 verses is divided into 28 chapters. The first chapter deals with the nature of the आत्मन्, which is omniscient, omnipotent and omnipresent; which has no birth, no death, no bondage and no लिबेरतिओन् either. The second deals with the proofs for the same. Duality is born out of इग्नोरन्चे of the real nature of the one Divine. Incidentally, even the great अवधूत has hinted at the need for a spiritual guide (2.23) in realizing the आत्मन्. The next two chapters deal with the inner nature of the आत्मन् in highly poetical tones. The fifth chapter advises a man to avoid all lamentations, as the आत्मन् is the same in all conditions. The sixth chapter negates all kinds of distinctions whether of caste or family, of senses or their objects, of the मिन्द् or the intellect or their activities—because none of these exists when looked at from the standpoint of the आत्मन्. The seventh describes the state of the अवधूत. The eighth gives a definition of the word ‘avadhūta’ by interpreting each of the four syllables (a, va, dhū, ta) of that word.
See also AVADHŪTA and DATTĀTREYA.

Avanti
------------------------------------------
A well-known जनपद or a country, during the period of the Mahābhārata, it was also called Avantikā. It was located in western India in the present Ujjain-Mandhata region of Madhya Pradesh. Divided into two parts, the northern region had उज्जयिनी as its capital whereas the capital of the south was माहिष्मती (the modern Mandhata). It was being ruled by two brothers Vinda and Anuvinda. They were subdued by सहदेव, the last of the Pāṇḍava brothers and paid contributions towards the expenses of the राजसूय sacrifice.
It is considered to be one of the seven cities (mahāpuṇyanagarīs) that confer great merit on those that dwell in it. It was here that सान्दीपनि lived and, बलराम and कृष्ण were educated. The people of this region were known to be great warriors, being the descendants of Haihayas, the most celebrated of whom was कार्तवीर्यार्जुन. Later on, it became the home of Buddhist and Jaina learning.

Avadhūta Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is one of the minor उपनिषद्स् belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda and classed among the सṁन्यास उपनिषद्स्, i.e., उपनिषद्स् teaching सṁन्यास or stressing a life of renunciation. The text is a mixture of prose and poetry and has 36 verses/sections.
Sāṅkṛti approaches अवधूत Dattā-treya and questions him thus: ‘Who is an अवधूत? What is his mental state? What are his characteristics? What is saṁsaraṇa?’
Dattātreya replies: ‘An “avadhūta” is one who has identified himself with the (a =) “akṣara” or the indestructible ब्रह्मन्, who is (va =) “vareṇya” or excellent, who has destroyed all bonds of transmigration (dhū = dhūta-saṁsārabandhana) and has become the goal of the Upaniṣadic sentences like (ta =) “tat tvam asi.” ’ Since he has already realized the आत्मन् or the Self, there is no need for him of following the rules and regulations of वर्ण and आश्रम (castes and stages of life). Hence he is also called an ‘ativarṇāśramin’ (one who has transcended the वर्ण-आश्रम-system).
‘Immortality can be attained by renunciation alone and not by rituals or progeny or wealth.
‘ “Saṁsaraṇa” means moving freely among the ignorant people to destroy their इग्नोरन्चे of the Self.
‘He may move about stark naked, partially clad or well-clad.
‘He sacrifices only to the inner Self and is free from all actions.
‘Though experiencing objects of senses, he is not tainted by them even as the sun is not tainted by the nature of the objects upon which he shines.
‘He is not affected by the desires entering into him even as the ocean does not overflow by the waters of the rivers entering it.’
Then follow some verses describing the inner state of the अवधूत: ‘The highest truth is that there is no च्रेअतिओन्, nor any destruction. There is no sādhaka (spiritual aspirant) nor a mukta (the liberated one). Those interested in progeny or wealth or other things, may engage themselves in action and suffer transmigration. But I am ever filled with bliss. I am not interested even in sleep or begging for ड़ोओद्. I have no need for śravaṇa (listening to Vedāntic texts) or मनन (reflecting on them) or nidi-dhyāsana (meditation). Let prārabdha कर्म (results of actions of previous lives) take its own course. Though I am now liberated, there is no harm in my following the path prescribed by the śāstras or scriptures to set an example to the ignorant people. I am ever blessed since I know my Self and the bliss of ब्रह्मन् is being clearly experienced.’
The Upaniṣad closes with a phala-śruti (eulogy) of the results that can be obtained if this is studied and realized.

avatāra
(‘one who has descended’)
------------------------------------------
The concept of ‘avatāra’ (incarnation of the Divine) is one of the fundamental tenets of हिन्दुइस्म्. The locus classicus of the theory of अवतार is in the Bhagavad-gītā (4.5-8).
After creating this world, God sets it in motion and regulates it through the cosmic law known as ṛta, सत्य or धर्म. When the cosmic law, the ṛta, is comprehended by the intellect, it becomes ‘satya’ (truth). When life is regulated according to it, it becomes ‘dharma’ (righteousness, right conduct).
Since the human मिन्द् is a product of the three guṇas (sattva, रजस् and तमस्), it is subject to vicissitudes. In the beginning सत्त्व will have the upper hand and people will naturally be inclined towards धर्म. Hence life on earth moves smoothly in harmony and peace. Gradually, as रजस् and तमस् gain ascend-ance, people will incline towards evil; and this will upset the social equilibrium. Good people devoted to धर्म will be neutralised and made ineffective whereas the evil ones addicted to अधर्म or unrighteousness will rule the roost. At such critical periods in human history God decides to ‘come down’ (avatāra = coming down) in a human form (or even in a non-human form if that is necessary) and restore the spiritual and social equilibrium implied by the word ‘dharma.’
Though restoring धर्म is the primary concern of an अवतार, eliminating or chastising the wicked, and, protecting the good—being a necessary and integral part of this process—are also undertaken by him.
An अवतार is not just a जीव who has attained the state of लिबेरतिओन् and is eager to help mankind. He represents the direct descent of God himself to the human level in order to help the human beings to ascend to the divine level, of which the liberated सोउल् is a perfect example. A जीव is forced to take a body due to his past actions (prārabdha-कर्म) whereas the अवतार incarnates of his own free will for saving mankind. Consequently, he is always conscious of his mission and power. It is only he who can see both the Absolute (Brahman) and the manifested world simultaneously and can teach the world about the Absolute.
Vedānta admits of God’s manifestation as the world, his omniscience as also omnipotence and grace. Hence there is nothing unreasonable in the doctrine that he can also assume a special and unique form as अवतार, fully retaining चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् of the divinity from his very birth.
Another speciality of this doctrine is that God incarnates himself in response to the needs of the times wherever and whenever necessary. Hence there are no restrictions regarding either the number of incarnations or the place. The sole consideration is the decline of धर्म and the rise of अधर्म in opposition to it, to such an extent that the social equi-librium is badly disturbed.
The अवतार concept is probably suggested in the Ṛgveda itself (3.53.8; 6.47.18) where इन्द्र is said to be endowed with the mysterious power of assuming any form at will. Some of the avatāras mentioned in the lists of the ‘Daśāvatāras’ (ten incarnations) are met with in the earlier Vedic literature. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa mentions the story of Matsya (fish इन्चर्नतिओन्) as also of the कूर्म (tortoise इन्चर्नतिओन्) and of the Varāha (boar इन्चर्नतिओन्) (vide 1.8.1.1-6; 7.5.1.5; 14.1.2.11). The Vāmanāvatāra (dwarf इन्चर्नतिओन्) of विष्णु taking the three steps is also clearly mentioned in the same scriptures (1.2.5.1).
Coming to the age of the epics and the पुराणस् we find a tendency towards limiting the avatāras to ten (hence the name ‘Daśāvatāras’ or ten incarnations) the last one (Kalki) being yet to come. The दशावतारस् are: Matsya (the fish), कूर्म (the tortoise), Varāha (the boar), नरसिṁह (the man-lion), वामन (the dwarf), परशुराम (Rāma with the battle-axe), राम (the son of दशरथ), कृष्ण (the son of Vasudeva), बुद्ध (Gautama बुद्ध) and कल्कि. However, there is no unanimity or uniformity in the various lists given by these works. Around the tenth century A. D., बुद्ध seems to have gained a place in the lists as the ninth इन्चर्नतिओन्. In the earlier lists as also the later ones, बुद्ध has been replaced by बलराम (Rāma of strength, elder brother of कृष्ण). Some lists include both बलराम and बुद्ध but omit कृष्ण, the raison d’etre being that all the ten are the avatāras of कृष्ण who is the Lord विष्णु Himself.
Sometimes we come across many more avatāras than the traditional ten. For instance, the Bhāgavata gives three lists of 22 names (1.3.6-22), 23 names (2.7.1 ff.) and 16 names (11.4.3 ff.) and also declares that the avatāras are innumerable (1.3.26).
Occasionally the avatāras are classified into three types: पूर्णावतार, अṁशावतार and आवेशावतार. Pūrṇāva-tāras are those in which the manifestation of the Divine is full and complete (pūrṇa = full) as in राम and कृष्ण. Aṁśāva-tāras are partial manifestations (aṁśa = part) of the Divine as in great sages like व्यास. Āveśāvatāras are those in which there is a temporary entry of the Divine (āveśa = entry) as in the case of Nṛsiṁha manifesting through पद्मपाद (a disciple of शङ्कर) who was a votary of that deity.

āvaraṇa
(‘veil, cover’)
------------------------------------------
Derived from the root ‘vṛ’ and with a prefix ‘ā,’ the word ‘āvaraṇa’ means anything which covers or surrounds. In the Advaita Vedānta it refers to the veiling power of māyā/avidyā. (See ĀVARAṆA-शक्ति.)
In temple architecture, it refers to the enclosures or prākāras, surrounding the main shrine, wherein the आवरण-देवतास् (minor deities, the attendants of the chief deity) are housed, as also the उत्सवमूर्ति (procession deity) and other paraphernalia.
In वीरशैविस्म् the word is used for a protective covering, in the spiritual sense. There are eight such āvaraṇas. (See AṢṬĀVARAṆAS.)

avasthā-traya
(‘three states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्’)
------------------------------------------
Works of Vedānta based primarily on the teachings of the उपनिषद्स्, recognize three ‘avasthās’ or states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् with which we are all familiar: जाग्रत् (waking state), स्वप्न (dream state) and सुषुप्ति (deep-sleep state). In the jāgrad avasthā both the sense-organs and the मिन्द् are active. In the स्वप्न-avasthā it is only the मिन्द्, impelled by the latent impression of the waking experience, and, sometimes, by the latent impressions of past lives, that is active. In the सुषुप्ति-avasthā, even the मिन्द् is at rest.
In all these three states there is always a ‘witness,’ called ‘sākṣi-चैतन्य,’ who is ever present as an observer, who also experiences the effects of these states. He is the आत्मन् or the Self.
Since he is, apparently, the ‘fourth’ (as opposed to the three states) he is called the ‘turīya’ (= the fourth). However ‘turīya’ is not considered as a state of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् but चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् itself.
An analysis of the three states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् leading to the establishment of the आत्मन् through reasoning, is called ‘avasthā-traya-विवेक’ or ‘avasthā-traya-vivecana.’
This subject has been dealt with in detail in the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad and the Kārikās of गौडपाद (A. D. 780).

avadhūta
(‘one who has shaken off [the worldly bonds]’)
------------------------------------------
The word ‘avadhūta,’ often met with in the Hindu religious literature, generally refers to a perfect man, also called a ‘paramahaṁsa’ or an ‘ativarṇāśramin.’ The Bhāgavata (skandha 11, chapters, 7, 8 and 9) mentions an अवधूत who had twentyfour teachers. The list includes the पञ्चभूतस् or the five elements, animals like elephant and deer, and human beings like a maiden and a child. He says that he learnt a lesson each, from each of them through careful observations.
The Avadhūtagītā, a work ascribed to अवधूत दत्तात्रेय, gives a description of the characteristics of an अवधूत, based on the four syllables—a, va, dhū and ta (8.5-9): He is free from desires. Ever pure, he lives in bliss. His speech is faultless. He has no body-चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. His मिन्द् is ever absorbed in ब्रह्मन् and hence he has no need to practise meditation. He is totally free from egoism and इग्नोरन्चे.
Avadhūta दत्तात्रेय has been mentioned in several उपनिषद्स्.
In a more restricted sense, the term ‘avadhūta’ is applied to the senior Nāgā साधुस् of the daśanāmī orders living in holy places like Rishikesh. They may or may not be naked. But they wear matted hair, necklace of रुद्राक्ष beads or even bones, and are indifferent to rules of observance common to other monastic or religious orders. Several types have been noted among them: Brahma-अवधूत, शिव-अवधूत, भक्त-अवधूत and हṁस-अवधूत.
The avadhūtas base their practices on the तन्त्रस्.
Female अस्चेतिच्स् of this variety are also known to exist and are called ‘avadhūtānīs.’
See also DAŚANĀMĪS and DATTĀTREYA.

avabhṛtha
(‘that which is pushed down or sunk’)
------------------------------------------
Avabhṛtha is the final purificatory bath marking the end of सोमयाग. This is an ‘iṣṭi,’ a rite needing four priests. After a number of preliminary rites in the याग-शाला (sacrificial shed), the yajamāna or sacrificer and his wife proceed to a flowing river or any reservoir, along with the priests, for the final bath and disposal of the utensils used in the sacrifice, as also other objects like the antelope skin and योक्त्र (cord of muñja grass worn by the wife). The utensils are smeared with the सोम juice before disposal. The rite itself takes place in water, a handful of कुश grass thrown on the water serving as the आहवनीय fire for that purpose. A special सामन् called अवभृथ-सामन्, is chanted during the rite.
The word ‘avabhṛtha-स्नान’ is also used to indicate the ceremonial bath at the conclusion of any major religious rite like the consecration of a new temple.

āvāhana
(‘invitation’)
------------------------------------------
During the वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्, gods have to be invited to come to the yāgaśālā or the sacrificial shed, to receive their share of the offerings. During the śrāddha or obsequial rites, the पितृस् or manes have to be invited to come and receive their offerings. Both these are done with appro-priate mantras. This act of inviting is technically called ‘āvāhana.’
Āvāhana is also done during the consecration of an image in a temple. The deity is invoked to come in its subtle form and reside in that image permanently, receiving worship and conferring boons.
In पूजा or ritualistic worship, आवाहन is considered as one of the उपचारस् or items of service to honour the deity. The particular मुद्रा or handpose exhibited during the act is called ‘āvāhanī-मुद्रा.’
